title: Not all effects reduce to heaven; soul, angels, demons; contingent modification
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): yet from ye defectibility belonging toward inferiors they are modified toward contingency — Therefore although in heaven ye aspects belonging toward stars are necessary. as is plain from meteorology — otherwise weak plus contingent — plus otherwise it receives heaven's action strong plus necessary — Next, because ye matter into which heaven acts is disposed in a varied mode. therefore not every effect belonging toward heaven is necessary. plus helping themselves by hidden modes through prayers poured toward God — First, because human souls, angels plus demons within ye order belonging toward concausing things, with Augustine plus Boethius witnessing, are not subjected toward heaven except accidentally. But because not all effects can be reduced toward heaven, there remain still other contingencies with respect toward heaven.
pass_b_english: But because not all effects can be reduced to heaven, other contingencies still remain with respect to heaven. First, because human souls, angels, and demons within the order of concausing things — as Augustine and Boethius witness — are not subjected to heaven except accidentally, inasmuch as the soul bound to bodies is affected through organs according to sense — and they themselves can master sense by repressing anger, shaking off sloth, perceiving remedies against plague and other deadly influxes of heaven, and helping themselves by hidden modes through prayers poured out to God. Therefore not every effect of heaven is necessary.

Next, because the matter on which heaven acts is variously disposed, and otherwise receives heaven's action as strong and necessary, otherwise as weak and contingent, as is plain from meteorology. Therefore although the aspects of the stars in heaven are necessary, yet from the defectibility of inferior things they are modified unto contingency.
source_text: Sed quia non omnes effectus ad caelum possunt reduci, remanent adhuc alia contingentia respectu caeli. Primo, quia animae humanae, angeli et daemones intra ordinem rerum concausantium, teste Augustino et Boethio, non subduntur caelo nisi per accidens, quatenus anima corporibus alligata per organa affecta secundum sensum afficitur — et ipsae possunt dominari sensui, reprimendo iram, excutiendo pigritiam, et percipiendo remedia contra pestem et alios letiferos caeli influxus, et adiuvando occultis modis seipsas per preces ad Deum fusas. Idcirco non omnis caeli effectus est necessarius. Deinde, quia materia in quam agit caelum est vario modo disposita, aliterque suscipit actionem caeli validam et necessariam, aliter imbecillam et contingentem, ut patet ex meteorologia. Ergo licet in caelo siderum aspectus sint necessario, tamen ex defectibilitate inferiorum modificantur ad contingentiam.
